title: The Full Transformer
oneLineScope: The encoder–decoder stack as published in Vaswani et al. 2017, assembled end to end.
prose:
Where we are. Every part is now on the table. The previous node gave us the transformer block — a self-attention sublayer and a position-wise FFN, each wrapped in a residual and layer norm — and we know how it is built from scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention, and positional encoding. What we have not yet done is wire the blocks into a complete, working model. The block left open the obvious question: a stack of blocks reads a sequence, but how does it produce one, and how do two sequences (a source and a translation) get connected?

The gist. The full transformer answers that by stacking the blocks into two towers. An encoder reads the entire input sequence at once; a decoder generates the output sequence one token at a time. The decoder block carries two extra ingredients beyond the encoder’s: a masked self-attention that forbids a position from peeking at its own future, and an encoder–decoder cross-attention that lets each output position reach back into the encoded source. Token ids come in through a learned embedding plus positional encoding; a linear projection and softmax over the vocabulary turn the decoder’s top vectors back into next-token probabilities on the way out.

Why it matters. This is the architecture Vaswani et al. actually published in 2017 — the reference design every later model is described against. Its shape is one you know cold from statistical machine translation: read a source sentence whole, then generate a target sentence one token at a time, each new token conditioned on the source and on what has been generated so far. What is new is that attention does all of the conditioning, and there is no recurrence anywhere. Strip away one tower or the other and you get the single-stack models — GPT, BERT — that the rest of the tutorial follows.

The two stacks

The model is two towers. The encoder is a stack of \(N\) identical transformer blocks of the previous node — self-attention then FFN, each wrapped in residual-plus-LayerNorm (the base model uses \(N = 6\)). It reads the entire source sequence at once; its self-attention is unmasked, so every source position may attend to every other in both directions. The output of the top encoder block is a sequence of \(n\) vectors, each of width \(d_{\text{model}}\), a context-rich re-representation of the source. That output is computed once and then held fixed while the target is generated.

The decoder is also a stack of \(N\) blocks, but each decoder block has three sublayers rather than two, each again wrapped in residual-plus-LayerNorm:

  1. Masked self-attention. The decoder attends over the target tokens generated so far — but with the causal mask from the scaled-dot-product node: position \(t\) may attend to positions \(1,\ldots,t\) and no further. Scores above the diagonal are set to \(-\infty\) before the softmax, so a token cannot see its own future. This is what makes generation left-to-right and well defined.
  2. Encoder–decoder cross-attention. This is the bridge between the towers, and it is worth recognizing what it is: exactly the Bahdanau-style alignment from the neural-MT node, now a first-class sublayer. The queries come from the decoder (the partial target), while the keys and values come from the top encoder output (the fixed source representation). So each target position issues a query and pulls a content-weighted blend of source positions — soft, learned alignment of target to source, the same operation the IBM models estimated with EM, here computed on the fly and trained end to end. The mask is dropped: a target token may align to any source token.
  3. Position-wise FFN. Identical in form to the encoder's — the per-token nonlinear computation.

The two towers thus differ in exactly two ways: the decoder's self-attention is causally masked, and the decoder carries the extra cross-attention sublayer that reads the encoder. Everything else — the FFN, the residuals, the LayerNorm, the width \(d_{\text{model}}\) — is shared design.

Seen from one step back, the architecture uses the same attention operation in three distinct roles, and naming them keeps the picture straight. Encoder self-attention is unmasked and stays within the source: queries, keys, and values all come from the source sequence, so each source token is re-expressed in terms of all the others. Decoder masked self-attention is the same, within the target, but causally masked so the past cannot read the future. Cross-attention is the only sublayer that spans the two sequences — queries from the target, keys and values from the source. Three uses, one mechanism; the differences are entirely in where the three inputs come from and whether a mask is applied. That economy — one operation, reused — is a large part of why the design is called what it is.

One consequence worth noting about cross-attention: because the keys and values are the fixed encoder output, the source need be encoded only once, no matter how long the generated target grows. Every decoder block, at every generation step, attends back into that same cached representation. This is the architectural payoff over the recurrent encoder–decoders it replaced, where the entire source had to be compressed into a single fixed-width vector that the decoder then leaned on; here the decoder keeps full, addressable access to every source position throughout generation.

Input and output plumbing

Tokens are not vectors, so both towers begin the same way. Each input token id indexes a learned embedding table \(E \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d_{\text{model}}}\) (\(V\) is the vocabulary size), producing one \(d_{\text{model}}\)-vector per token; the positional encoding of the previous-but-one node is then added, since attention alone is order-blind. That sum, an \(n \times d_{\text{model}}\) matrix, is what enters the bottom block of each stack.

At the top of the decoder, each output position holds a \(d_{\text{model}}\)-vector that must become a distribution over the vocabulary. A single learned linear projection to \(V\) logits, followed by a softmax, does it: the result is \(P(\text{next token} \mid \text{context}) \in \mathbb{R}^{V}\), a proper next-token distribution of the kind you know from \(n\)-gram language models, only now conditioned on the full source and target-so-far. The paper ties the weights of this output projection to the input embedding table \(E\) (the same matrix, transposed) — it both saves \(V \times d_{\text{model}}\) parameters and reflects a genuine symmetry, that the geometry mapping a token to its vector should relate to the geometry scoring a vector against tokens. (The paper also scales the embeddings by \(\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}\) before adding the positional encoding, a small bookkeeping detail that keeps the embedded signal and the positional signal at comparable magnitude.)

Training: teacher forcing

The model is trained by teacher forcing, a name for a practice you would recognize immediately. Rather than feed the decoder its own (early, wrong) predictions during training, you feed it the true target sequence, shifted right by one position so that at step \(t\) the decoder sees the real tokens \(1,\ldots,t-1\) and must predict token \(t\). The causal mask is what makes this safe to do for the whole sequence in one parallel pass: each position is structurally forbidden from seeing the answer it is being asked to produce. The loss is ordinary cross-entropy between the predicted distribution and the true next token, summed over positions — the negative log-likelihood of the target sequence under the model. At inference time the crutch is gone: there is no true sequence, so the decoder consumes its own previous outputs, generating left to right one token at a time. This is the gap teacher forcing leaves open — train on the gold prefix, test on the model's own prefix — and the resulting train/test mismatch (small early errors compounding as they feed back in) is a known cost of the method, the price paid for the parallel, fully-supervised training pass it buys. The encoder, by contrast, has no such asymmetry: it sees the same complete source at training and inference alike.

The base model, in numbers

The configuration to anchor on, all attributed to the paper, is: \(d_{\text{model}} = 512\), \(h = 8\) heads (so \(d_k = d_v = 64\)), \(N = 6\) blocks per stack, and \(d_{\text{ff}} = 2048\) inside each FFN. That is the “base” transformer, about 65 million parameters. (They also report a “big” variant with wider layers.) These are not magic numbers — they were tuned for the WMT translation benchmarks of the day — but they are the reference point every later model is described against, so they are worth committing to memory. A useful sanity check on the parameter count: with two stacks of six blocks and \(d_{\text{model}} = 512\), each block holds on the order of three million parameters (the bulk in the FFN), and the embedding/projection table adds \(V \times d_{\text{model}}\) on top; for a vocabulary in the tens of thousands the totals land near the quoted 65 million. The scale is modest by what came later — these models trained on a handful of GPUs in a few days — which is part of why the architecture's reach was such a surprise.

Where it connects

This encoder–decoder is the complete published architecture, but it is not the only way to wire the pieces, and the field quickly specialized. Drop the encoder and the cross-attention and keep only the masked decoder stack, and you have a pure left-to-right language model — the autoregressive LM (the GPT line). Drop the decoder and the mask and keep only the bidirectional encoder, and you have masked LM (BERT). When to prefer the full encoder–decoder over either single-tower design is exactly the question the encoder–decoder contrast node takes up.

diagrams.caption: The full encoder–decoder transformer (Figure-1 style): an N-deep encoder on the left feeds the cross-attention of an N-deep decoder on the right; both start from embeddings plus positional encoding, and the decoder ends in a linear projection and softmax over the vocabulary.
diagrams.altText: A two-tower diagram. On the left, the encoder: an input sequence of token embeddings has positional encoding added, then flows up through a stack of N identical encoder blocks, each containing self-attention and a feed-forward network with Add and Norm. On the right, the decoder: the right-shifted output embeddings have positional encoding added, then flow up through a stack of N decoder blocks, each containing masked self-attention, then encoder–decoder cross-attention, then a feed-forward network, each wrapped in Add and Norm. Arrows run from the top of the encoder stack horizontally into the cross-attention sublayer of every decoder block, supplying keys and values. Above the decoder, a linear layer projects to V logits followed by a softmax, producing the output-token probabilities. Shapes n by d_model are labeled on the streams.
diagrams.prompt: Structural diagram, Figure-1 style, of the full encoder–decoder transformer, drawn as two vertical towers side by side, flow bottom to top. LEFT TOWER (the encoder): at the bottom, 'Inputs' (source tokens) lead into an 'Input Embedding' box; a small circle labeled '+' adds 'Positional Encoding' to it. The sum (label the stream 'n x d_model') flows up into a stack drawn as a box labeled 'Encoder block' containing, stacked, 'Multi-Head Self-Attention' then 'Add & Norm' then 'Feed-Forward (FFN)' then 'Add & Norm'; mark the whole stack 'x N (= 6)'. RIGHT TOWER (the decoder): at the bottom, 'Outputs (shifted right)' lead into an 'Output Embedding' box; a '+' circle adds 'Positional Encoding'. The sum flows up into a stack labeled 'Decoder block' containing, stacked: 'Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention' (annotate 'causal mask') then 'Add & Norm', then 'Encoder-Decoder Cross-Attention' then 'Add & Norm', then 'Feed-Forward (FFN)' then 'Add & Norm'; mark the stack 'x N (= 6)'. Draw a prominent horizontal arrow from the TOP of the encoder stack into the 'Encoder-Decoder Cross-Attention' sublayer of the decoder, labeled 'keys & values from encoder'; and a short arrow into the same sublayer from below labeled 'queries from decoder'. Above the decoder stack: an arrow into a box 'Linear' (annotate 'to V logits'), then into a box 'Softmax', producing 'Output probabilities' (annotate 'P(next token), size V') at the top. Emphasize the cross-attention link between the towers as the bridge. Structural diagram: the two-vs-three sublayer difference, the causal mask on decoder self-attention, and the encoder-to-decoder cross-attention arrow must be exact.

diagrams.caption: Encoder–decoder cross-attention: queries come from the decoder, keys and values from the top encoder output. Each target position pulls a weighted blend of source representations — learned, soft target-to-source alignment.
diagrams.altText: A diagram of the cross-attention sublayer. On the right, the decoder's current hidden state (n_target by d_model) is projected by W_Q into queries Q (n_target by d_k). On the left, the top encoder output (n_source by d_model) is projected by W_K and W_V into keys K (n_source by d_k) and values V (n_source by d_v). Q and K feed a matmul producing scores of shape n_target by n_source, scaled by one over root d_k, passed through a row-wise softmax to attention weights A (n_target by n_source), then multiplied by V to give the context output (n_target by d_v). A note marks this as the same soft-alignment operation as Bahdanau attention.
diagrams.prompt: Structural data-flow diagram of encoder-decoder cross-attention, showing where queries, keys, and values come from. On the RIGHT, a matrix labeled 'decoder hidden state' with shape n_target by d_model; an arrow labeled 'x W_Q' leads to a matrix Q with shape n_target by d_k (the queries). On the LEFT, a matrix labeled 'encoder output (top block)' with shape n_source by d_model; two arrows labeled 'x W_K' and 'x W_V' lead to matrices K (shape n_source by d_k) and V (shape n_source by d_v). Q and K feed a matrix-multiply box producing a score matrix with shape n_target by n_source; an arrow labeled 'divide by root d_k' leads to a box 'softmax (row-wise)' annotated 'each row sums to 1', producing attention weights A with shape n_target by n_source. A and V feed a final matrix-multiply producing the output 'context' with shape n_target by d_v. Add a margin note with a leader line reading: 'queries from the decoder, keys & values from the encoder — soft target-to-source alignment, exactly Bahdanau attention'. Emphasize that the score matrix is n_target by n_source (rectangular, not square). Label every matrix with its name and shape. Structural diagram: the source of Q vs. K/V and all shapes must be exact.

bibliography.citation: Vaswani, A., et al. (2017). "Attention Is All You Need." NeurIPS.
bibliography.annotation: The whole of §3 and Figure 1 are this node. §3.1 gives the encoder and decoder stacks and the three decoder sublayers; §3.2.3 specifies the three uses of attention (encoder self, decoder masked self, encoder-decoder cross); §3.4 covers the embeddings, the tied output projection, and the softmax; §5.1 lists the base hyperparameters (d_model=512, h=8, N=6, d_ff=2048) and Table 3 the parameter counts.

bibliography.citation: Rush, A., et al. "The Annotated Transformer."
bibliography.annotation: A complete, runnable PyTorch reimplementation of the paper, section by section. The EncoderDecoder, Encoder/Decoder stacks, the masking, the Generator (linear + softmax), and the full training loop with label-smoothed cross-entropy are all here. The best source for seeing teacher forcing and the masks as actual code.

The clearest visual walk-through of the encoder/decoder assembly and how the fixed encoder output feeds every decoder block's cross-attention. Start here for the geometry of the data flow before reading §3 of the paper.
